title: House Prices — Tidymodels Tour
text:
This site is a guided tour of the Kaggle Housing Prices Competition for Kaggle Learn Users — the Ames, Iowa house-price dataset — worked end to end in R with the tidymodels framework. It is written for an R user who is comfortable with the language and with statistics, but is new to Kaggle — so we narrate the competition workflow as well as the modelling reasoning, and we lean on ggplot2 for every chart.
It is the regression companion to the classification-flavoured Titanic tour: same structure, same tidymodels muscle memory, different problem shape.



You get a training set (data/raw/train.csv, 1460 houses) where the outcome is known: the SalePrice in dollars.
You get a test set (data/raw/test.csv, 1459 houses) with the same 79 features but no SalePrice.
Your job: predict SalePrice for every test house, write those predictions to a CSV (Id,SalePrice), and upload it. Kaggle scores your CSV and places you on the leaderboard.







TipThe metric shapes everything



Submissions are scored on Root-Mean-Squared-Error between the logarithm of the predicted and the logarithm of the observed SalePrice. Taking logs means an error on a cheap house counts as much as a proportional error on an expensive one. So throughout this project we model log(SalePrice) — which makes each model’s cross-validated rmse directly comparable to the leaderboard score.

title: House Prices — Tidymodels Tour
text:
The goal
Predict SalePrice for the 1459 test houses as accurately as possible (lowest log-RMSE), and document the reasoning so the whole thing is reproducible and teachable.
We fit six different model families on identical features so they can be compared apples-to-apples, then blend them in a stacked ensemble:

Random Forest

Elastic Net

How the documents link together
This is a small Quarto website. index.qmd (this page) is the master document; everything else lives in docs/ and the navbar ties them into a narrative:
Home (index) → EDA → Models {XGBoost, RF, Neural Net, Elastic Net, SVM, MARS} → Stack → Submission → Kaggle Setup

Model docs — each follows the same structure (recipe → spec → workflow → tune → finalize → evaluate → save), so once you’ve read one, the others are easy to skim.
Submission — a single parameterized document that turns any saved model into a leaderboard-ready CSV.
Kaggle Setup — authenticate the Kaggle CLI.

title: House Prices — Tidymodels Tour
text:
How to reproduce
Everything is pinned with renv and uses here::here() for paths, so there is no setwd() fragility.

Restore the environment:
renv::restore()
Get the data — the CSVs ship in data/raw/; or follow the Kaggle setup guide to pull the official files.
Render the site. Because of freeze: auto, the heavy model fits only run the first time (or when a model doc changes):
quarto render
Logical run order: EDA → each base model doc (each saves its tuning result and fitted workflow to models/) → stack → submission.







Note



set.seed(42) is set in R/00_setup.R and the resampling folds are seeded, so CV results are reproducible across machines that share the renv lockfile.

title: House Prices — Tidymodels Tour
text:
Results summary
The table below compares the six base models on cross-validated rmse and rsq, read directly from each model’s saved tuning results (models/*_res.rds), so they update automatically on every render. No copying. The rmse is on the log(SalePrice) scale — the same units as the Kaggle leaderboard.


Show code
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(here)

# Pull the best (rmse-selected) configuration's CV metrics from a saved
# tune_grid result.
cv_metrics <- function(path, label, notes) {
  res  <- readRDS(path)
  best <- select_best(res, metric = "rmse")
  m    <- collect_metrics(res) |> semi_join(best, by = names(best))
  tibble(
    Model           = label,
    `CV RMSE (log)` = m$mean[m$.metric == "rmse"],
    `CV R-squared`  = m$mean[m$.metric == "rsq"],
    `Best num_comp` = best$num_comp,
    Notes           = notes
  )
}

bind_rows(
  cv_metrics(here("models", "xgboost_res.rds"), "XGBoost",
             "tuned trees / tree_depth / learn_rate / min_n + num_comp"),
  cv_metrics(here("models", "rf_res.rds"), "Random Forest",
             "tuned mtry / min_n + num_comp; 1000 trees"),
  cv_metrics(here("models", "nnet_res.rds"), "Neural Net",
             "tuned hidden_units / penalty + num_comp; PCA-normalized"),
  cv_metrics(here("models", "elasticnet_res.rds"), "Elastic Net",
             "glmnet: tuned penalty / mixture + num_comp"),
  cv_metrics(here("models", "svm_res.rds"), "SVM (RBF)",
             "kernlab: tuned cost / rbf_sigma + num_comp"),
  cv_metrics(here("models", "mars_res.rds"), "MARS",
             "earth: tuned num_terms / prod_degree + num_comp")
) |>
  arrange(`CV RMSE (log)`) |>

The submission workflow at a glance
Once a model is fitted and saved (each model doc does this), turning it into a leaderboard entry is mechanical and wrapped in the parameterized submission document:
quarto render docs/submission.qmd -P model:xgboost
quarto render docs/submission.qmd -P model:stack
That loads models/<model>_fit.rds, predicts on the test set, exponentiates the log predictions back to dollars, writes models/submission_<model>.csv (Id, SalePrice), and prints the exact kaggle competitions submit command.

title: Building a Kaggle Submission
section: How to render this document per model
text:
How to render this document per model
This .qmd has a model parameter (default "xgboost"). Override it on the command line with -P model:<value>:
quarto render docs/submission.qmd -P model:xgboost
quarto render docs/submission.qmd -P model:rf
quarto render docs/submission.qmd -P model:nnet
quarto render docs/submission.qmd -P model:elasticnet
quarto render docs/submission.qmd -P model:svm
quarto render docs/submission.qmd -P model:mars
quarto render docs/submission.qmd -P model:stack
Each render reads the matching models/<model>_fit.rds, writes models/submission_<model>.csv, and prints the exact upload command. You must have fitted (rendered) the corresponding model document first so the .rds exists.

requested_model <- params$model

# This single lookup table is the source of truth for which models are submittable.

  xgboost    = here::here("models", "xgboost_fit.rds"),
  rf         = here::here("models", "rf_fit.rds"),
  nnet       = here::here("models", "nnet_fit.rds"),
  elasticnet = here::here("models", "elasticnet_fit.rds"),
  svm        = here::here("models", "svm_fit.rds"),
  mars       = here::here("models", "mars_fit.rds"),

if (!requested_model %in% names(model_paths)) {

    "Unknown model '", requested_model, "'. ",

title: Model 6 — MARS

Why MARS?
MARS fits the response as a sum of hinge functions — piecewise-linear splines with automatically chosen knots — and can multiply them for interactions. That makes it naturally suited to housing data, where a feature’s effect often changes slope at a threshold (e.g. living area matters more up to a point). It is nonlinear yet interpretable, and diverse from the trees. We tune the number of retained terms and the interaction degree.

title: Model 4 — Elastic Net

Why elastic net?
A regularised linear model is the classic, interpretable regression baseline — and on the log scale, with the Yeo-Johnson-transformed features from the recipe, it is genuinely competitive on Ames. glmnet blends ridge (L2) and lasso (L1) penalties: penalty sets the total shrinkage and mixture the L1/L2 balance (1 = pure lasso, 0 = pure ridge). Lasso also does automatic feature selection, which is handy given ~200 dummy columns.

title: Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
The target: SalePrice is right-skewed


Show code

  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = house_pal[1]) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = dollar) +
  labs(title = "SalePrice", x = NULL, y = "Count")

  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = house_pal[2]) +

SalePrice (left) is right-skewed; log(SalePrice) (right) is close to normal.




This single fact drives the whole project: prices span an order of magnitude and are right-skewed, so we model log(SalePrice). Conveniently, Kaggle scores the competition on RMSE of the log price — so training on the log scale optimises the leaderboard metric directly. range(SalePrice) is roughly $34,900 – $755,000.

title: Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
First look: structure and missingness


Show code
train |>
  summarise(across(everything(), ~ mean(is.na(.x)))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "pct_missing") |>
  filter(pct_missing > 0) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(variable, pct_missing), y = pct_missing)) +
  geom_col(fill = house_pal[1]) +
  geom_text(aes(label = percent(pct_missing, accuracy = 1)), hjust = -0.1, size = 3) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent, expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Missingness by column", x = NULL, y = "Missing")





Columns with missing values. Most ‘missingness’ is really absence.




The crucial Ames gotcha: for most of these columns NA does not mean “unknown”, it means “the feature is absent”. PoolQC is missing for 99.5% of houses because almost no house has a pool; Alley NA means no alley access; GarageType/BsmtQual NA means no garage/basement. Blindly imputing these would invent features that aren’t there. So R/03_engineer.R recodes them:

Categorical absent → "None" (Alley, PoolQC, Fence, all the Bsmt/Garage quality columns, FireplaceQu, MasVnrType, MiscFeature).
Numeric absent → 0 (GarageArea, GarageCars, MasVnrArea, all the basement square-footages).
Genuinely missing → impute in the recipe. Only LotFrontage (~18%) and a handful of one-off stray NAs in the test set (MSZoning, KitchenQual, …) are truly unknown; those get KNN / median / mode imputation inside every CV fold.

title: Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
What predicts price?

Overall quality


Show code
train |>
  mutate(OverallQual = factor(OverallQual)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = OverallQual, y = SalePrice, fill = OverallQual)) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = dollar) +
  labs(title = "Overall quality is the single strongest predictor",
       x = "OverallQual (1–10)", y = "SalePrice")





SalePrice rises steeply and monotonically with OverallQual.




OverallQual — the rater’s 1–10 judgement of material and finish — is the strongest single predictor in the data, and nearly log-linear against price.


Living area


Show code
ggplot(train, aes(x = GrLivArea, y = SalePrice)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, colour = house_pal[1]) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, colour = house_pal[3], se = FALSE) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = dollar) +
  labs(title = "Bigger houses cost more (mostly)",
       x = "GrLivArea (sq ft)", y = "SalePrice")





Above-grade living area vs price. Note the two high-area/low-price outliers.




Living area is strongly linear against price. The two houses bottom-right (huge but cheap) are the well-known Ames outliers — partial sales. We leave them in and let the log transform + robust models absorb them, but they are worth knowing about. This motivates the engineered TotalSF (basement + 1st + 2nd floor).


Neighborhood


Show code
train |>
  group_by(Neighborhood) |>
  summarise(med = median(SalePrice), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(Neighborhood, med), y = med, fill = med)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = dollar) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Median price by neighborhood",
       x = NULL, y = "Median SalePrice")





Median SalePrice by neighborhood — location, location, location.




Neighborhood spreads median price roughly 3× from cheapest to dearest — a strong categorical the recipe dummy-encodes (lumping the rarest levels into "Rare").


Age


Show code
train |>
  ggplot(aes(x = YearBuilt, y = SalePrice)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.35, colour = house_pal[4]) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", formula = y ~ x, colour = house_pal[3], se = FALSE) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = dollar) +
  labs(title = "Price by year built", x = "YearBuilt", y = "SalePrice")





Newer houses sell for more; the relationship is nonlinear.




Age matters, nonlinearly — motivating the engineered HouseAge, RemodAge, and an IsNew flag.

title: Exploratory Data Analysis
section: What this means for the recipe
text:
What this means for the recipe
Everything above justifies the two-stage feature pipeline:

R/03_engineer.R (deterministic, up front): recode NA → "None"/0 for absent features; derive TotalSF, TotalBath, TotalPorchSF, HouseAge, RemodAge, and the Has*/Is* flags; treat MSSubClass as categorical.
make_recipe() (estimated per CV fold): KNN-impute LotFrontage, median/mode-impute stray NAs, Yeo-Johnson the skewed numerics, lump rare factor levels, dummy-encode, normalize, and append principal components.







Note



The scale-sensitive models (neural net, SVM, elastic net) rely on the step_normalize() + step_YeoJohnson() in the recipe; the tree ensembles are scale-invariant and ignore them harmlessly.

title: Model 5 — Support Vector Machine (RBF)

Why an SVM?
Support vector regression with a radial-basis kernel draws a smooth, nonlinear response surface over the normalized principal components. Its errors are structurally different from the trees’ and the linear model’s — diversity that pays off in the stack. It needs scaled inputs, which the shared recipe already provides. We tune the regularisation cost and the kernel width rbf_sigma.

title: Model 7 — Stacked Ensemble
text: Where we are: The capstone of the House Prices — Tidymodels Tour. The six base-model documents (XGBoost, Random Forest, Neural Net, Elastic Net, SVM, MARS) each saved their tuning results (every candidate model and its out-of-fold predictions) to models/<model>_res.rds. Here we feed all of those candidates to stacks, which learns a regularised linear blend over them — usually beating any single model, because the members make different mistakes.

title: Model 7 — Stacked Ensemble
text:
Why stack?
Each model family has a different inductive bias: gradient boosting chases interactions, the random forest averages decorrelated trees, the neural net and SVM learn smooth functions of the principal components, the elastic net is linear, MARS is piecewise-linear. A stack fits a meta-learner (penalised linear regression) on the members’ out-of-fold predictions, keeping only the candidates that pull their weight. Everything stays on the log(SalePrice) scale until the final submission.

section: 1. Create a Kaggle account and accept the rules
text:
1. Create a Kaggle account and accept the rules

Sign up at https://www.kaggle.com (free; Google sign-in works).
Go to the competition page: https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/home-data-for-ml-course.
Click Join Competition and accept the rules. You must do this — the API will refuse to download data or accept submissions until you have accepted the competition rules in the browser.

2. Generate your API token (kaggle.json)

Click your avatar (top right) → Settings.
Scroll to the API section → Create New Token.
Your browser downloads kaggle.json (username + secret key — treat it like a password, never commit it).
Move it into place and lock down the permissions:
mkdir -p ~/.kaggle
mv ~/Downloads/kaggle.json ~/.kaggle/
chmod 600 ~/.kaggle/kaggle.json

The chmod 600 step matters — the CLI warns (and on some systems refuses to run) if the file is world-readable.

3. Verify the CLI
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"   # add to ~/.bashrc to make it permanent
kaggle --version

4. Download the data the “real” way
Once authenticated, pull the official competition files:
kaggle competitions download -c home-data-for-ml-course -p data/raw
unzip data/raw/home-data-for-ml-course.zip -d data/raw
This gives you data/raw/train.csv (1460 rows, includes SalePrice), data/raw/test.csv (1459 rows, no SalePrice), sample_submission.csv, and data_description.txt. These overwrite the mirror copies — that is fine, they are the same data.

5. Submit predictions to the leaderboard
The Quarto submission document generates one CSV per model into models/, named submission_<model>.csv where <model> is one of xgboost, rf, nnet, elasticnet, svm, mars, or stack. Each file has exactly two columns — Id,SalePrice — one row per test house, with SalePrice in dollars.
General form:
kaggle competitions submit -c home-data-for-ml-course -f models/submission_<model>.csv -m "<message>"
Concrete examples:
kaggle competitions submit -c home-data-for-ml-course -f models/submission_xgboost.csv -m "xgboost baseline"
kaggle competitions submit -c home-data-for-ml-course -f models/submission_stack.csv  -m "stacked ensemble"
The -m message shows up next to your score so you can tell submissions apart.

section: 6. Check your score and submission history
text:
6. Check your score and submission history
kaggle competitions submissions -c home-data-for-ml-course
kaggle competitions leaderboard  -c home-data-for-ml-course --show
The score is RMSE on log(SalePrice) — lower is better. A stacked tidymodels ensemble on these features typically lands around 0.12–0.13.
